source_text: Nec in uno hoc aut alio fuit ista dignatio. Namque Aemilianus, quamuis equestris ordinis gentiliter haberetur, unus tamen in carcere et ipse de fratribus, qui ad quinquagesimum prope aetatis annum carnis continentia puer uenerat, continuatis in carcere gemina superpositione ieiuniis et orationibus saepe repetitis, per quas deuota mens pasta in alium diem sacramento domini parabatur, in somno die medio reclinatus, mox quiete discussa talia nobis suae uisionis arcana patefecit. Producto mihi, inquit, e carcere homo gentilis, hoc est frater meus carnalis, occurrit. In res nostras admodum curiosus insultabunda uoce perquirit, sciscitans quatenus nos in illis poenalibus tenebris et inedia carceris haberemur. Cui responsum dedi, milites Christi et in tenebris clarissimam lucem et in ieiunio cibum saturabilem dei habere sermonem. Et cum haec audisset, Scitote, inquit, quod omnes uos qui in carcere habemini, si obnixe perstabitis, manebit poena capitalis. At ego qui uerebar ne conpositum luderet fraude mendacium, confirmare uotum meum uolui et Vere, inquam, patiemur omnes? At ille rursus affirmat: Gladius uobis et sanguis in proximo est. Sed uelim scire, inquit, an omnibus uobis, qui uitam istam contempnitis, indiscreta et aequalia munerum caelestium praemia rependantur. Cui responsum dedi: Non sum idoneus huius tam magnae rei ferre sententiam. Attolle, inquam, oculos paulisper ad caelum: iam uidebis innumerabilem turbam micantium siderum. Numquid stella omnis pari luminis honore praefulget? Et tamen lumen omnibus unum est. Ad haec ille curiosius iterum quod interrogaret inuenit. Ergo si qua discretio est, inquit, qui uestrum sunt in promerenda domini uoluntate potiores? Nimirum, inquam, prae ceteris duo, quorum nec tibi dicenda et deo nota sunt nomina. Nouissime incumbenti acrius et perscrutanti molestius, Ii sunt, inquam, qui quo difficilius et tardius uincunt, gloriosius coronantur; et propter hoc scriptum est: Facilius intrabit camelus per foramen acus, quam diues in regna caelorum.
thought_title: Aemilianus reports his midday dream about rewards
orientation: Aemilianus, a fellow prisoner with Marian and James, tells the brothers a dream in which his pagan blood brother questions him about prison and heavenly rewards.
pass_a_gloss: Nor was this gracious favor in this one man or in another alone. For Aemilianus, although in pagan estimation he was held to be of equestrian rank, yet himself also one of the brothers in prison, who to nearly the fiftieth year of his age had come as a boy by continence of the flesh, with fasts continued in prison by a double added fast and with prayers often repeated, through which the devout mind fed was being prepared unto another day for the solemn pledge of the Lord, reclined in sleep in the middle of the day, soon when sleep was shaken off laid open to us such secrets of his vision. When I had been led out of prison, he said, a pagan man, that is my brother by flesh, met me. Very curious about our affairs he inquires with a mocking voice, asking how we were faring in those penal darkness and in the starvation of prison. To him I gave answer, that soldiers of Christ have both in darkness a most bright light and in fasting the word of God as filling food. And when he had heard this, Know, he said, that for all you who are held in prison, if you persist firmly, a capital punishment waits. But I who feared lest a composed lie was mocking with deceit, wished to confirm my vow and Truly, I said, shall we all suffer? But he again asserts: Sword and blood for you is near. But I would like to know, he said, whether to all of you who despise this life undistinguished and equal rewards of heavenly gifts are repaid. To him I gave answer: I am not fit to pass judgment on so great a matter. Lift, I said, your eyes a little while to heaven: now you will see an innumerable crowd of glittering stars. Does every star shine forth with equal honor of light? And yet the light for all is one. At this he found again with more curiosity something to ask. Therefore if there is any distinction, he said, who of you are superior in earning the will of the Lord? Clearly, I said, two before the rest, whose names are both not to be told to you and known to God. At last to him pressing on more keenly and searching more importunately, They are, I said, those who by as much as they conquer with more difficulty and more slowness, by so much are crowned more gloriously; and on account of this it is written: More easily will a camel enter through the hole of a needle than a rich man into the kingdoms of the heavens.

pass_b_english: Nor was this gracious favor given to one man or another alone. Aemilianus shared it in prison as well. Though in pagan estimation he was held to be of equestrian rank, he was still one of the brothers there. By continence of the flesh he had come to nearly his fiftieth year as a boy. In prison he kept fast upon fast with doubled fasting and prayers repeated again and again. Through them his devout mind was fed and made ready for another day for the solemn pledge of the Lord. At midday he lay down in sleep. Then, as soon as sleep left him, he opened to us the secrets of his vision.

"When I had been led out of prison," Aemilianus said, "a pagan man met me, that is my own blood brother. He was full of curiosity about our affairs, and he pressed me in a mocking voice. He wanted to know how we were faring in that punishing darkness and in the starvation of prison. I answered him, 'Soldiers of Christ have a most brilliant light even in darkness, and the word of God as satisfying food even in fasting.' When he heard this, he said, 'Know that all of you who are held in prison will face the death penalty if you persist resolutely.'"

"I feared he might be playing a composed lie with deceit," Aemilianus said, "so I wanted to make my hope sure. 'Shall we truly all suffer?' I asked. But he affirmed again, 'Sword and blood are near for you. Yet I would like to know whether all of you who despise this life are repaid with heavenly rewards that are undistinguished and equal.' I answered him, 'I am not fit to pass judgment on so great a matter. Lift your eyes to heaven for a little while. Now you will see a countless crowd of glittering stars. Does every star shine forth with equal honor of light? And yet the light for all is one.' At this he found with still more curiosity another question to ask. 'If there is any distinction,' he said, 'who among you are foremost in earning the will of the Lord by service?' 'Certainly above the rest there are two,' I said, 'whose names must not be told to you and are known to God.'"

"When he still pressed me harder and probed me more importunately," Aemilianus said, "I told him, 'They are those who, the more hardly and slowly they conquer, are crowned more gloriously. And for this it is written: It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:24).'"
